details:
**Willy Loman's suicide by car crash for life insurance**
Willy Loman, an aging, failing traveling salesman, deliberately crashes his car offstage so his family can collect a $20,000 life insurance policy. He hopes the money will let his son Biff succeed. Earlier he tells his neighbor Charley that he is "worth more dead than alive."

**"The Woman" in Boston and the silk stockings**
In a flashback, teenage Biff goes to Willy's Boston hotel and finds him with a mistress known only as "The Woman." Willy had given her new silk stockings while his wife Linda mends her old ones, and he grows angry whenever he sees Linda mending. Willy pleads "She's nothing to me... I was lonely," but Biff is shattered, calls him a fake, and loses his faith in his father.

**Biff steals Bill Oliver's fountain pen**
Biff waits all day to ask his former employer Bill Oliver for a business loan, but Oliver barely remembers him. Biff impulsively steals Oliver's fountain pen and runs "down eleven flights with a pen in [his] hand." The theft fits Biff's lifelong habit of stealing, including a football from his high school and a carton of basketballs from Oliver.

**Biff flunks math and burns his "University of Virginia" sneakers**
Biff was a star high school football player who had printed "University of Virginia" on his sneakers. After he failed math and then discovered Willy's affair in Boston, he burned the sneakers in the furnace. He never retook the class or went to college, which ended his football future.

**Uncle Ben: "the jungle is dark but full of diamonds"**
Ben is Willy's dead older brother, who appears in Willy's hallucinations. Ben boasts, "When I was seventeen I walked into the jungle, and when I was twenty-one I walked out. And by God I was rich!" He set out for Alaska but ended up in Africa and made a fortune in diamonds, and Willy forever regrets refusing Ben's offer of work in Alaska. Flute music accompanies Willy's memories of his family.

**Howard Wagner, the wire recorder, and "a man is not a piece of fruit"**
Howard is Willy's young boss and the son of Frank Wagner, the man who first hired Willy. When Willy asks for a non-traveling job in New York, Howard is busy showing off a recording of his son reciting state capitals ("The capital of Ohio is Cincinnati..."), and he then fires Willy. Willy protests, "You can't eat the orange and throw the peel away—a man is not a piece of fruit!" He also invokes Dave Singleman, an old salesman who sold from his hotel room and died "the death of a salesman."

**Frank's Chop House and the waiter Stanley**
Willy meets his sons Biff and Happy at this restaurant. Biff struggles to admit that Oliver turned him down, while Happy keeps covering up the bad news. Happy picks up two women, Miss Forsythe and Letta, and the sons abandon Willy, who is left babbling in the restroom. The waiter Stanley finds him there.

**Bernard and the Supreme Court**
Bernard is Charley's studious son, who once tried to help Biff with his math and was mocked by Willy as "liked, but not well liked." He grows up to become a successful lawyer about to argue a case before the Supreme Court, which makes Willy envious. Bernard tells Willy about Biff burning his sneakers.

**The "Florida idea" sporting-goods plan**
Happy proposes that he and Biff sell sporting goods together under the Loman Brothers name. This plan is why Biff seeks the loan from Bill Oliver. The idea briefly revives Willy's hopes before it collapses.

**Planting seeds at night: "I don't have a thing in the ground"**
At the Chop House, Willy suddenly asks Stanley where he can buy seeds, lamenting that nothing is planted. Late that night he plants them by flashlight in his yard while talking to Ben. The garden can't grow because high-rise apartments now block the sunlight where elm trees once stood.

**The Requiem and Linda's "We're free"**
The play's short final scene is the "Requiem," held at Willy's funeral. Biff says Willy "had the wrong dreams," and Charley defends him: "A salesman is got to dream, boy. It comes with the territory." Linda sobs that she made the last mortgage payment that day, repeating "We're free."

**Charley, the neighbor**
Charley plays cards with Willy and secretly lends him money, including money for his insurance premium. He offers Willy a job, which Willy proudly refuses. Willy scorns Charley because he can't put up a ceiling, saying "A man who can't handle tools is not a man... You're disgusting."

**"Well liked"**
Willy's core belief is that success comes from being "well liked" and having personal charm. He tells his sons that Bernard is "liked, but not well liked." Charley mocks this belief by pointing out that J.P. Morgan wasn't successful because he was well liked.

**The rubber hose in the cellar**
Linda finds a short rubber hose hidden in the cellar, attached near the gas heater, which shows that Willy has been planning suicide. Biff later confronts Willy by throwing the hose in front of him. In the same confrontation Biff reveals he spent three months in jail for stealing a suit in Kansas City.

**"Attention must be paid"**
Linda says this line to her sons, insisting that Willy deserves respect despite his flaws: "He's not the finest character that ever lived. But he's a human being... So attention must be paid." It is one of the play's most famous lines.
